children: By Joe Stonor
Anthropic is set to beat out its rival OpenAI to one of the largest initial-public offerings in history. The key to winning the race: taking the lion's share of the enterprise market.

OpenAI still leads on consumer-facing artificial intelligence, but Anthropic's Claude has become the darling of businesses. That success drove Anthropic's revenue to around $17 billion in the third quarter of 2026, around $7 billion more than its main rival.

Now, Anthropic is on the precipice of a public offering that could raise about $1.5 trillion to $1.6 trillion, while OpenAI deferred its IPO to next year. Anthropic itself hones in on enterprise as the driver of its success, putting its precipitous revenue growth down to Claude experiencing "the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology in history," according to the company's Securities and Exchange Commission filing.

It wasn't a race Anthropic always looked set to win, but the company has seen a stark run up in demand from businesses. The turnaround in fortunes can be seen in microcosm from data collected by Vertice, a London procurement company with more than 400 clients that spend about $75 billion on AI solutions.

A year ago, Vertice clients spent about ten times more on OpenAI than they did on Anthropic. Now, OpenAI's advantage hasn't only been eroded, but reversed entirely. In October, Anthropic got 72% of the money Vertice clients spent across both model makers--up from 10% a year ago.

As the world's leading frontier model makers, Anthropic and OpenAI are locked in a high-stakes race for market share. While some observers bet the two companies might segment the market--with OpenAI leaning toward courting consumers--both are zeroing in on also dominating the lucrative enterprise market.

Anthropic and OpenAI didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. In public comments, Anthropic has heralded its success among enterprises, while OpenAI has said it is redoubling its efforts in the area.
So far, Anthropic's relentless focus on businesses and the success of its popular coding tool Claude Code have given it the edge over its rival.

Earlier this year, Chris Barrett, operations head at German-headquartered software-as-a-service company Staffbase, was mulling which AI-model maker to pick for his business. He ran tests and sounded out colleagues. The results were clear: Anthropic's Claude was more accurate, easier to use and smoother to integrate than its competitors.

"It was so easy on Claude, people didn't even really try to test that much on OpenAI anymore because they were getting good results in a much more efficient and quicker manner, in a very user-friendly way," Barrett said.

OpenAI isn't taking its competitor's success lying down. The maker of ChatGPT has responded by doubling down on efforts to lure enterprise customers, including cutting prices in a bid to grow market share, The Wall Street Journal has reported.

The company's agentic software coding tools--a crucial capability for enterprise--are gaining traction. OpenAI's revenue from enterprise overtook revenue from its consumer business for the first time in the third quarter, co-founder and President Greg Brockman told the WSJ Tech conference earlier this month.
OpenAI still holds the lead among financial-services clients, according to Vertice analysis of its clients' spending. And among consumers, ChatGPT remains synonymous with large-language models.
The company continues to target a 2027 IPO, the company's Chief Financial Officer Sarah Friar told CNBC earlier this month.

Still, Anthropic's dominance over enterprise spending on AI looks entrenched. In the week ending Nov. 1, just shy of 50% of business spend on AI tokens went to Anthropic, according to data from the Federal Reserve's online data base, FRED, and collected by business-services company Ramp from its more than 85,000 customers. The last time ChatGPT OpenAI led on that metric was September 2025.
The Ramp data reflects what some analysts and procurement specialists say: AI contracts are sticky.

AI offerings from across the market are attractive, Staffbase's Barrett said. But after spending months building its workflows and employee skills on Claude, the cost of switching would be high. In the company's office, "Claude" is now as interchangeable with AI as "Google" is with internet search, he said.

"Claude itself has just become so sticky so fast, much stickier than any other tool," said Barrett. "If we're going to make a switch to something else, it has to be worth not only its cost, but also the disruption we would have within the business."

Data from Vertice showed that not only do customers opt for Anthropic over OpenAI more often, they spend more with Anthropic than its competitor. More than five times as many companies commit $250,000 or more a year to Anthropic as they do to OpenAI, the data showed.
As the two frontier model makers fight for AI dominance, they should avoid becoming complacent, said Giles Tulloch, a portfolio manager and technology specialist at investment house J. Stern & Co.
Data from both Ramp and Vertice show that, up to this point, enterprise spending on AI has gone to either OpenAI or Anthropic. But open-source model makers are slowly growing in revenue.
"Going forward, the debate isn't going to be OpenAI versus Anthropic. It's more: OpenAI and Anthropic versus open-source," Tulloch said.
